entries.definition: A GSAT variant that mixes a uniformly chosen flip from the distinct variables currently occurring in unsatisfied clauses with a globally best GSAT flip, using a fixed probability to choose the focused random move.
entries.identity_notes: This is the mixed random-walk extension of GSAT described by Selman and Kautz and clarified in the later noise paper. Its focused move samples a duplicate-free union of eligible variables, not a clause followed by one of its variables. The latter distribution underlies the separately described WSAT family. It is also distinct from unrestricted GSAT random noise and from a pure clause-first walk for 2-SAT. No normalized identity match was found across all 442 pinned AIO labels/scoped synonyms and 316 preceding native IDs/names/aliases. Full-checkout fixed-string searches included ignored and hidden files in worktree and main, returning 7 and 7 lines respectively. All seven unique lines were inspected, and the sorted checkout hit sets were identical: neighboring GSAT/WalkSAT mentions and saved review/ledger references, not existing candidate records. Eight exact AIO CLASS nodes with scoped synonyms/comments and outgoing edges and four full native neighboring records were inspected. Absence is bounded to this snapshot and semantic neighborhood.
limitations: The focused random branch and the global greedy branch use different candidate sets. Replacing the former by random-clause-then-random-variable sampling changes the transition distribution, even at p=1. Shared behavior at p=0 does not make the full variant identical to basic GSAT.

Finite search failure is not a proof of unsatisfiability. The polynomial analysis cited for pure random walks on satisfiable 2-CNF does not establish a corresponding general-CNF bound for this mixture.

The noise parameter, CNF encoding, initialization and outer budgets affect behavior. No single best p, universal speedup or numerical benchmark claim is curated. Empty clauses or empty candidate sets require explicit handling outside the described nonempty-variable flip rule.

claims.statement: Maintain a complete assignment of the variables in the input CNF formula. Stop successfully when it satisfies the formula. Otherwise, with fixed probability p, select uniformly from the distinct variables appearing in at least one currently unsatisfied clause and flip the chosen variable. With probability 1−p, evaluate all single-variable flips and choose a largest increase in the total number of satisfied clauses, breaking tied best choices randomly as in GSAT. The random and greedy branches can make non-improving moves. The extension can use the GSAT outer random-initialization, per-attempt flip budget and restart/attempt budget. The 1994 paper explicitly explains the duplicate-free variable list, which gives equal probabilities to eligible variables even when their clause occurrence counts differ.

entries.name: WalkSAT
entries.definition: A clause-focused SAT local-search algorithm, in its classical SKC formulation, that first selects an unsatisfied clause, prioritizes a variable with zero breakcount, and otherwise mixes a random variable flip with a minimum-breakcount flip within that clause.
entries.identity_notes: This record curates the classical SKC variable-selection rule under the commonly used WalkSAT name. It does not equate every later WalkSAT heuristic, the earlier underspecified WSAT family description, pure clause-first random walk, or global GSAT-with-walk selection with that exact rule. The 1994 source gives the clause-first lineage; the authors’ 2004 solver description explicitly supplies the zero-break priority and breakcount-based choice. No normalized identity match was found across all 442 pinned AIO labels/scoped synonyms and 316 preceding native IDs/names/aliases. Full-checkout fixed-string searches included ignored and hidden files in worktree and main, returning 7 and 7 lines respectively. All seven unique lines were inspected, and the sorted checkout hit sets were identical: neighboring GSAT/WalkSAT mentions and saved review/ledger references, not existing candidate records. Eight exact AIO CLASS nodes with scoped synonyms/comments and outgoing edges and four full native neighboring records were inspected. Absence is bounded to this snapshot and semantic neighborhood.
limitations: The zero-break branch precedes the noise coin, including at p=1. That setting is therefore not generally identical to a pure random-clause/random-variable walk. Removing the priority changes the specified SKC heuristic.

Candidate selection is restricted to the chosen clause and can miss the globally best net-gain flip. Minimizing breakcount is different from minimizing breakcount minus makecount; replacing one by the other changes the heuristic.

A finite unsuccessful run does not prove UNSAT, and the pure 2-CNF random-walk guarantee is not automatically a guarantee for this SKC policy on general formulas. The noise setting and restart strategy are not universal constants.

The move rule needs a nonempty selected clause and a declared formula representation. Empty clauses require separate handling; duplicate clauses, literal normalization and weighted extensions can change counts or sampling and are not silently normalized here.

AutoWalksat, Rnovelty, Rnovelty+ and later software additions are distinct procedures or configurations, not exact aliases of this SKC record. No author implementation or numerical solver benchmark was run.

claims.statement: Maintain a complete truth assignment and stop successfully when all clauses are satisfied. Otherwise randomly choose an unsatisfied nonempty clause. For each candidate variable in that clause, its breakcount is the number of currently satisfied clauses that would become unsatisfied if it were flipped. If any candidate has breakcount zero, choose one such candidate at random. Only when there is no zero-break candidate, choose a random variable from the selected clause with probability p; with probability 1−p choose a candidate of minimum breakcount, breaking ties randomly. Flip the chosen variable and repeat under the application’s stopping budget. Breakcount omits how many previously unsatisfied clauses become satisfied, so it need not rank candidates like GSAT’s global net-gain score. Random restarts are an optional outer strategy; the described 2004 competition configuration uses one long run.

definition.val: A layer that is a densely-connected neural network layer with added noise for regularization.

comments: Noisy dense layer that injects random noise to the weights of dense layer. Noisy dense layers are fully connected layers whose weights and biases are augmented by factorised Gaussian noise. A NoisyDense layer implements the operation: $$ mathrm{NoisyDense}(x) = mathrm{activation}(mathrm{dot}(x, mu + (sigma cdot epsilon)) mathrm{bias}) $$ where mu is the standard weights layer, epsilon is the factorised Gaussian noise, and delta is a second weights layer which controls epsilon.

limitations: GSAT is an incomplete model finder under finite budgets. A satisfiable formula may be missed, and the source discusses families that can require exponentially many attempts. Search failure must not be reported as an UNSAT proof.
Allowing plateau and occasionally decreasing flips distinguishes the method from strict-improvement hill climbing. Replacing these moves with immediate restarts changes the specified procedure.

claims.statement: For up to MAX-TRIES attempts, generate a random complete truth assignment for the input CNF clauses. A returned assignment is a directly checkable model; an unsuccessful search does not prove unsatisfiability. native_neighbors.name: Simulated annealing
native_neighbors.definition: A stochastic optimization procedure that explores candidate configurations with temperature-controlled acceptance of cost-increasing moves and progressively cools that acceptance process to concentrate search on low-cost configurations.
native_neighbors.identity_notes: This record denotes the temperature-scheduled optimization procedure exemplified by Kirkpatrick, Gelatt and Vecchi. Its basic symmetric-proposal Metropolis step is distinguished from fixed-temperature target sampling, generic annealing metaphors, training signal annealing and a proof that a particular finite schedule reaches a global minimum. The 1983 article is a primary formulation, not a claim of exclusive invention. No normalized identity match was found across all 442 pinned AIO labels/scoped synonyms and 285 preceding native IDs/names/aliases. Full-checkout fixed-string searches included ignored and hidden files in worktree and main, returning 15 and 15 lines respectively. Every text hit was a prior candidate lead. Nine exact AIO CLASS nodes with scoped synonyms/comments and outgoing edges and seven native neighboring mechanisms were inspected. Absence is bounded to this snapshot and semantic neighborhood.
limitations: The exp(−delta/T) expression is for positive effective temperature with the physical Boltzmann constant absorbed into its cost units. Zero temperature is a limiting or separately defined greedy rule, not evaluation of that quotient at T=0. Equal-cost moves are accepted in the displayed symmetric-proposal rule.

At fixed T the Boltzmann interpretation requires a proper target and a valid transition construction. Arbitrary asymmetric proposals do not justify dropping the reverse-to-forward proposal ratio. Lowering T changes the target; stationarity for a fixed stage does not imply equilibrium throughout a finite cooling run.

Positive-temperature uphill acceptance only permits escape through moves supported by the proposal. It does not ensure reaching every state, escaping a local basin in a chosen budget or tracking equilibrium. Rapid cooling can freeze search prematurely; schedule length, cost scale, move connectivity and constraints matter.

The primary article’s heuristics and empirical scaling claims are not a finite-run global-convergence theorem or a universal complexity bound. The later mathematical conditions for asymptotic annealing convergence were not audited here. No electronic-design or traveling-salesman benchmark is reproduced.

claims.statement: Choose a representation of feasible configurations, an objective E to minimize, a random rearrangement proposal and an annealing schedule specifying temperatures and work at each temperature. At current configuration x, propose y and compute delta=E(y)−E(x). For the basic symmetric-proposal Metropolis rule at effective temperature T>0 measured in cost units, accept delta<=0 moves and accept delta>0 with probability exp(−delta/T); otherwise retain x. Repeat transitions at the current temperature, then lower temperature according to the schedule. High temperatures permit larger cost-increasing moves more frequently; cooling reduces that probability. The source motivates sufficient equilibration at each stage. Candidate representation, move set and schedule depend on the optimization problem; the returned low-cost configuration is a search result rather than a certified global minimizer.

limitations: The state representation and sampling process must support the controlled Markov assumptions. Partial observability, changing dynamics, biased sample reuse or unvisited actions prevent importing the stated theorem unchanged. Infinite visits alone are insufficient without the learning-rate conditions.

A fixed positive learning rate violates the finite squared-sum condition; neural or other function approximation is not covered by the tabular theorem. The record does not claim all such variants fail, only that this particular guarantee does not establish their convergence.

The action-replay process in the proof is an analytical construction, not a required replay-buffer implementation. Section 4 separately discusses reusing empirical samples and warns that repeated reuse can favor the observed empirical environment. DQN’s additional machinery is not silently included.

The paper sketches undiscounted absorbing and multiple-entry extensions but does not establish every multi-step variant under the displayed theorem. Discounting, available actions, ties, terminal representation and initialization need a declared application. The proof’s full appendix was not independently audited; no benchmark claim is curated.

claims.statement: Maintain a finite table Q(x,a). On a sampled transition with current state x, action a, reward r and next state y, change only that entry to (1−alpha)*Q(x,a)+alpha*(r+gamma*max_b Q(y,b)), using the pre-update table for the target; leave other entries unchanged. Repeated samples supply rewards and next states without requiring an explicit estimated transition model. The maximum defines a greedy target even when behavior chooses an exploratory action; the update itself does not prescribe an exploration policy. In the paper’s discounted finite Markov setting, 0<gamma<1. Its theorem reports almost-sure convergence to optimal action values under bounded rewards, table representation, infinitely many samples of each state-action pair, and per-pair learning-rate sequences whose sum diverges while their squared sum converges, with 0<=alpha<1. This is an asymptotic, assumption-dependent statement, not a finite-sample stopping certificate.
